source.title: Inference and learning in sparse autoencoders as natural gradient flow
source.authors: Hadi Vafaii; Tejas Rao; David Chanin; Thomas Fel; Jacob L. Yates; Bruno Olshausen; David Klindt; Dileep George; Miguel Lázaro-Gredilla

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present. Some tables and figures are flattened in the text, but the relevant table entries are assignable.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses synthetic sparse-feature data with controlled overlap and evaluates feature recovery, including an ablation of lateral interactions. It also evaluates SAE features on language-model activations using probing and intervention benchmarks. These are conceptual tests, not a reproduction of the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: Rows below cover the paper’s own synthetic feature-recovery results, lateral-interaction ablation, full-width synthetic results, and Gemma SAE evaluation. Theoretical derivations are not empirical rows. Results cited from other studies are not rows. The Gemma metrics assess what SAE features can do in probing and interventions; they do not directly measure the model’s feature geometry.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes BeFOND, an iterative natural-gradient sparse coder, and reports how well it performs against other SAEs. Superposition is built into the synthetic data by construction: SynthSAEBench lowers the input dimension d at a fixed 16,384 features to raise overlap (ρmm). So the synthetic results measure how well each dictionary-learning method recovers known planted features, not whether networks store features in superposition. The Gemma-2-2B results (SAEBench sparse probing, RAVEL) compare SAE methods with each other. There is no control that could show sparse features are absent or present in the model. No result bears on toy-model geometry, on the capacity or other causes of polysemanticity, on whether SAE features are canonical or stable units, or on 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that unifying inference and learning as natural-gradient flows (BeFOND) gives explaining away that reduces interference between overlapping features. Fisher preconditioning compensates for rare features. BeFOND improves synthetic dictionary recovery and rare-feature detection, with a growing advantage as overlap increases. On Gemma-2-2B it improves single-feature probing and RAVEL disentanglement, with gains growing with width and matching Gemma Scope with about 1,000× fewer tokens.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes BeFOND, a Bernoulli iterative sparse-coding model with natural-gradient inference and dictionary learning, and evaluates it with SynthSAEBench and SAEBench; it does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments or geometry measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Synthetic recovery changes as input dimension and feature overlap change; lateral-interaction type affects recovery. On Gemma, probing and RAVEL scores vary with dictionary width and metric.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic data with planted overlapping features, recovery of the true dictionary depends strongly on the SAE's inference and learning method. Amortized SAEs degrade sharply as overlap rises: JumpReLU MCC falls to about 0.56 at d=256. Iterative inference with lateral suppression degrades only modestly (about 0.78). Removing suppression drops MCC to 0.28.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well dictionary learning recovers superposed features depends on the inference method. Single-projection encoders provably cannot compute exact posteriors for overlapping atoms.

fits_no_version.finding: Rare features are recovered far worse by standard SAEs than by Fisher-preconditioned learning in the full-width synthetic setting: Rare F1 0.30 for BatchTopK vs 0.95 for BeFOND.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE recovery of rare features is limited by optimizer conditioning, not only by dictionary capacity.

record.problems: The synthetic MCC measure concerns alignment to ground-truth directions and does not measure pairwise angles or regular geometry. The Gemma evaluations are on one model and one layer; sparse probing and RAVEL provide indirect evidence about SAE features rather than direct observation of the model’s underlying feature geometry.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached. Omitted Table 4 entries include MCC results for the other synthetic methods and some additional comparator seeds; Table 4 also reports dead-latent counts by method and seed. Omitted Gemma Table 6 metrics include AUC, F1, five-feature probing, and the cause and isolation components reported alongside disentanglement. These were left out after retaining the BeFOND and BatchTopK single-feature accuracy and overall RAVEL results across widths, and the central synthetic sweep and ablation results.

untested.parts: All of it. No toy network is trained to store features; there are no measurements of near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent phase transitions, or regular geometry.
Whether LLM features are spread across neurons, and whether recoverable sparse features exist. The Gemma results only rank SAE methods on downstream benchmarks.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. Method and width dependence of feature quality is reported only as a performance comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader classified this as T2 'tests' with V1/V4 supports. That is wrong: superposition is an assumption built into the benchmark, and all rows are the study's method compared against baselines. Row ranges are given as grouped row_ids.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests recovery as overlap increases and reports rare-feature recovery, but does not measure whether learned directions are nearly orthogonal, a sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or regular geometric arrangements.
The paper does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from competition for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.

The study tests SAE-feature concept detection and selective intervention on Gemma-2-2B activations. It does not directly measure feature distribution across neurons or independently establish that the SAE features exhaustively recover model features.
No test of SAE features as complete, stable, canonical units is reported.
The study uses dictionary atoms and synthetic ground-truth feature directions, but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations in the language model.
